title: Google's Switch Transformer: one expert per token, scaled to 1.6 trillion parameters
summary: Switch Transformer simplifies MoE's top-k expert routing to a single expert—just 1 instead of k—then adds capacity limits, a simplified load-balancing loss, and a set of training-stability tricks. We work through the capacity factor and balancing loss by hand, and lay out the speedups over T5, the distillation and multilingual results, and the paradox that more parameters don't always mean better downstream performance.
ai_summary: Switch Transformers (Fedus, Zoph, Shazeer; Google; JMLR 2022) simplifies mixture-of-experts layers into Switch layers that route each token to a single expert—just 1—replacing some of T5's feed-forward networks. The paper uses expert capacity and a capacity factor to handle dynamic routing, uses a single auxiliary loss for load balancing, and proposes selective float32 precision inside the router, smaller initialization, and expert dropout. At the same per-token FLOPs, pretraining is up to 7x faster than T5-Base; it beats mT5-Base on all 101 languages; and the 1.6-trillion-parameter Switch-C is 4x faster than T5-XXL. Distillation preserves about 30% of the gains, but larger models don't necessarily win on reasoning-heavy downstream tasks.
brief: Problem: MoE's complexity, communication costs, and training instability have kept it from being widely adopted.
Method: send each token to one expert; set an expert capacity; use a single load-balancing loss; and apply selective precision in the router, smaller initialization, and expert dropout.
Results: up to 7x faster pretraining than T5-Base at the same FLOPs; gains across all 101 languages; and a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that is 4x faster than T5-XXL.
Limitations: the largest dense-compute version is still unstable; upstream perplexity gains don't always transfer to reasoning-heavy downstream tasks; distillation keeps only about 30% of the gains.

paper.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
paper.authors: William Fedus, Barret Zoph, Noam Shazeer

cover.headline: A close read of the Switch Transformers paper

nodes.label: The router picks only one expert

sections.h: The bottom line: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: Google's William Fedus, Barret Zoph, and Noam Shazeer posted the paper in January 2021; it was published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR) in 2022. Shazeer was the first author of the earlier sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) paper and the second author of T5.

The earlier MoE work showed that parameters can be decoupled from compute, but it never became widely used. The paper names three reasons: **complexity, communication costs, and training instability**. Switch Transformer's goal is to make MoE simpler and more stable.

The central change is counterintuitively simple: **send each token to only one expert**. Earlier thinking held that the gating network needed to compare at least two experts to learn how to route; this paper finds that k = 1 not only works, but keeps quality, costs less compute, and is easier to implement. It replaces every other feed-forward network in T5 with a Switch layer and leaves the rest of the architecture unchanged.

Around that simplification, the paper provides a recipe for making sparse models train well: a simplified load-balancing loss, selective precision that uses high precision only inside the router, smaller initialization, and extra dropout inside the experts during fine-tuning.

The results: pretraining is up to 7x faster than T5-Base at the same FLOPs; it beats the multilingual baseline on all 101 languages; and a 1.6-trillion-parameter model reaches the same perplexity 4x faster than T5-XXL.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: Simplify MoE's top-k expert routing to a single expert—just 1—then add capacity limits, a load-balancing loss, and training-stability tricks. Parameters explode as experts are added, while per-token compute stays the same as a dense model.

callout.title: Three small concepts you'll need
callout.text: If you're not familiar with them, these three are enough:
list: **MoE layer**: many expert networks plus a gate (router); each input goes to only a few experts. See the close read on sparse mixture of experts (MoE).
**T5**: Google's encoder-decoder model, and the baseline for every comparison in this paper. See the T5 close read.
**FLOPs**: floating-point operations, a measure of compute. "Same FLOPs" is the premise behind all of this paper's comparisons.

sections.h: The Switch layer: each token goes to one expert

blocks.p: First, recall MoE routing. The router computes a set of scores for each token and runs them through a softmax to get a probability for every expert:

parts.desc: Probability token x is routed to expert i
The set of selected experts. Original MoE picks the top k (k ≥ 2); Switch picks only 1—the single highest-probability expert.
Expert output multiplied by its routing probability. Even with one expert, this multiplication gives the router a gradient.

formula.note: The paper argues that this multiply-by-gate-probability step is what makes a k = 1 router trainable, without the two-expert comparison earlier researchers thought was necessary.

plain.title: Only one appointment
plain.text: Each token arrives, the router W_r scores every expert, and it sends the token only to the highest-scoring one; the expert's output is then multiplied by that probability p. That multiplication is key: it lets the router know whether it sent the token correctly, so it can learn how to route.

blocks.p: The paper lists three benefits of k = 1:

list: **Less routing computation**: each token goes to only one expert.
**Each expert's batch size can at least be halved**: each token occupies one slot, not k slots.
**Simpler implementation, less communication**: in distributed training, each token only needs to be sent to one device.

callout.title: Like a hospital where each patient gets only one appointment
callout.text: In the earlier MoE, triage sends each patient to two or three doctors and then combines their weighted opinions. Switch triage gives out only one appointment, with the best-suited doctor. Intuition says you lose some benefit of a second opinion, but experiments found almost no loss, while the hospital itself becomes much simpler and cheaper to run.

sections.h: Capacity: how many tokens each expert can take

blocks.p: TPUs require every tensor shape to be fixed at compile time, but routing is dynamic: you don't know in advance how many tokens in each batch will go to which expert. So every expert needs a fixed **capacity**:

formula.expr: expert capacity = (tokens per batch / number of experts) × capacity factor

parts.sym: tokens per batch / number of experts
parts.desc: How many tokens each expert would get under perfectly even routing
How much extra headroom. Greater than 1 so experts can absorb somewhat uneven routing.

formula.note: Tokens beyond capacity are "dropped": this layer doesn't process them, and they pass through the residual connection unchanged to the next layer. The paper says dropped tokens were usually under 1% in experiments.

plain.title: Every car has a fixed number of seats
plain.text: Think of each expert as a car with fixed seats (four, here). The router sends six people; four sit down, and the remaining two skip this layer and take the residual connection to the next. The capacity factor is like keeping extra empty seats: fewer people get left behind, but empty seats still take up space.

fig.title: Worked example: a larger capacity factor drops fewer tokens but wastes more slots
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: a batch of 12 tokens and 3 experts; the router sends 6, 4, and 2 tokens to experts 1, 2, and 3. Numbers are ours, computed from Equation (3) and matching Figure 3.
fig.note: Larger capacity avoids dropping tokens, but empty slots still consume memory and take part in communication. The paper finds Switch performs better at smaller capacity factors (1.0, 1.25), which matters for memory-constrained large models.

blocks.p: The appendix also tries a "no token left behind" scheme: overflow tokens are redirected to the expert with the second-highest probability. It brings no practical benefit. The paper suspects that once the model learns token-expert assignments, sending a token to a different expert actually makes things worse.
The earlier MoE used two losses (importance and load). Switch combines them into one, computed for each Switch layer:

parts.desc: The fraction of the T tokens actually dispatched to expert i. It is counted, so it can't be differentiated.
The average router probability assigned to expert i across the batch. This one is differentiable.
Number of experts. Multiplying by N keeps the loss constant at α under uniform routing, independent of the number of experts.
Coefficient, set to 10^{-2} throughout: large enough to balance load, small enough not to overwhelm the main cross-entropy loss.

plain.title: Two sets of books: where tokens actually went, and where the router wanted to send them
plain.text: f is how many tokens each expert actually received in the batch (counted); P is how much probability the router on average wanted to give it (computed). Multiply them and sum: the more concentrated the assignment, the larger the loss. Because f can't be differentiated, the penalty works through P: the more tokens an expert actually receives, the harder its router probability is pushed down.

blocks.p: **How does it work?** Gradients only flow back through P_{i}, and the gradient with respect to P_{i} is proportional to f_{i}. So the more tokens an expert actually gets, the harder its router probability is pushed down, and later tokens are steered toward other experts.

fig.title: Worked example: more concentrated routing means a larger load-balancing loss
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: 4 experts, α = 0.01. The f and P numbers are ours, computed from Equations (4)–(6).
fig.note: When unbalanced, expert 1 has f = 0.70, so the gradient on P_{1} is largest and the router is pushed to send fewer tokens to expert 1.

blocks.p: The paper pretrains on C4 with T5's span-masking objective (masking 15%). All models use the same per-token FLOPs as T5-Base (MoE uses more because it routes to two experts), and they train for the same number of steps on the same 32 TPUv3 cores. All MoE and Switch models have 128 experts and place an expert layer at every other feed-forward network.

fig.title: Switch vs. MoE and T5: same hardware, speed and quality
fig.subtitle: From Table 1. Quality is negative log perplexity after 100k steps (closer to 0 is better); "time to target" is the hours needed to reach -1.50.
fig.note: At fixed compute and wall-clock time, Switch reaches the target fastest. The smaller the capacity factor, the clearer Switch's advantage over MoE. Switch-Base+ is a scaled-up Switch made as slow as MoE, and its per-step quality beats every model.

blocks.p: The paper also reports a surprise: when MoE's capacity factor drops from 2.0 to 1.25, speed falls from 840 to 790. The authors explain that speed depends on both the algorithm and low-level implementation optimizations.

sections.h: Three tricks for training sparse models well

blocks.p: **1. Selective precision.** Training in low precision like bfloat16 saves memory and communication, but the router's softmax and exponential operations are precision-sensitive and can destabilize training. Earlier work, GShard, had to use float32 throughout. Switch's solution: convert the input to float32 only inside the router function, then convert back to bfloat16. The expensive float32 tensors never travel between devices, yet you get float32 stability.

fig.title: High precision only inside the router is enough
fig.subtitle: From Table 2; early in training for 32-expert models

plain.title: Use the fine ruler only for the critical step
plain.text: Measuring a whole house needs only a normal tape measure; only the door-lock step needs calipers. Switch works the same way: the entire network uses memory-saving low precision, and only the error-prone steps inside the router (softmax, exponentials) temporarily switch to high precision before switching back.

blocks.p: **2. Smaller initialization.** Weights are initialized from a truncated normal with standard deviation √(s / n), where n is the input dimension. The paper suggests shrinking the Transformer default scale s = 1.0 by a factor of 10. After 3,500 steps, mean quality improves from -3.60 to -2.72, and the standard deviation across three random seeds drops from 0.68 to 0.01. The same scheme is used from 223M parameters all the way up to over a trillion.

**3. Expert dropout.** Switch has far more parameters than dense models with the same compute, so it overfits small downstream tasks more easily. Simply raising dropout everywhere hurts; the paper keeps non-expert layers at 0.1 and raises dropout only inside experts to 0.4.

fig.title: During fine-tuning, raise dropout only inside experts
fig.subtitle: From Table 4. d is ordinary dropout, ed is expert dropout.

blocks.p: The appendix also compares ways to make the router explore: always pick the top score, sample by probability, apply dropout to the input, and multiply the input by a random perturbation. It ends up choosing random perturbation (jitter).

sections.h: Scaling: more experts means more speed—even big dense models can't keep up

blocks.p: **By step count**: with per-token FLOPs fixed, experts increase from 2 to 256, parameters from 223M to 14.7B, and test loss keeps falling. The 64-expert Switch-Base reaches T5-Base's level at step 60k versus step 450k—7.5x faster by step count.

**By wall-clock time**: Switch adds routing computation and cross-device communication, so a step-count advantage doesn't automatically become a time advantage. But in fixed-time, fixed-compute measurements, 64-expert Switch-Base reaches T5-Base's perplexity in about one-seventh the time.

**Against a larger dense model**: what if you spend that compute training a bigger dense model, T5-Large? T5-Large uses 3.5x the FLOPs per token of Switch-Base, yet Switch-Base is still more sample-efficient and 2.5x faster by wall-clock time.

fig.title: Same FLOPs, parameters can differ by tens of times
fig.subtitle: From Table 9 (partial). FLOPs/seq is compute per sequence.
fig.note: Switch-C uses only about one-seventh the FLOPs per sequence of T5-XXL, yet has more than a hundred times the parameters; the paper says it reaches the same perplexity 4x faster.

blocks.p: The paper pretrains both T5 and Switch on an improved C4 for 550k steps and roughly 576B tokens, then fine-tunes them on various tasks.

fig.title: Fine-tuning results: better on most tasks, but not always on reasoning tasks
fig.subtitle: From Table 5 (partial), validation sets, higher is better
fig.note: SuperGLUE improves by 4.4 and 2 percentage points respectively; knowledge-focused tasks like closed-book QA improve especially strongly. Only ARC reasoning questions don't improve: Switch-Base underperforms T5-Base on the Challenge set, and Switch-Large underperforms T5-Large on the Easy set (the table shows only Challenge).

blocks.p: **Distillation**: Trillion-parameter models are hard to deploy, so can a large sparse model be compressed back into a small dense one? The paper finds two techniques useful: initialize the student with the non-expert weights of the teacher; and mix the teacher's probabilities with the true labels in the loss at a 0.25:0.75 ratio. This preserves about 30% of the quality gain.

fig.title: Distilling Switch back down to T5-Base size
fig.subtitle: From Table 7. "Retained" is the percentage of the teacher's quality gain over T5-Base that the student keeps.
fig.note: All students are the 223M-parameter T5-Base, whose own quality is -1.636. Even when compressed to 1% of the original size, it retains 28% of the teacher's gain.

blocks.p: **Multilingual**: After 1M pretraining steps on mC4 across 101 languages, Switch beats the FLOP-matched mT5-Base on **all** 101 languages, with an average 5x speedup and at least 4x in 91% of languages.

sections.h: Trillion-parameter models: combining three kinds of parallelism

blocks.p: Section 5 of the paper explains how to distribute the model across thousands of cores. Let the total number of cores be N = n × m, where n is the number of data-parallel replicas and m the number of model-parallel partitions:

list: **Data parallelism**: each core holds a full copy of the model and processes different data, synchronizing gradients only at the end of each step.
**Model parallelism**: split the feed-forward network's large matrices across cores; every layer's forward and backward pass requires an all-reduce communication.
**Expert parallelism**: each core holds different experts. Routing requires two all-to-all communications: send tokens to the core holding the expert, then send the results back.

plain.title: Three ways to divide the work
plain.text: Data parallelism: each chip holds a full model copy (M) and processes different data. Model parallelism: a model is sliced into parts (¼); each chip computes one part and they sync with each other frequently. Expert parallelism: each chip holds different experts (E1, E2, ...); tokens must first be sent to the chip holding the expert, then results are sent back.

blocks.p: Switch-C uses only expert and data parallelism, so its width and depth are far smaller than T5-XXL's; Switch-XXL has the same compute as T5-XXL but adds model-parallel communication overhead. After 250k training steps, both end up more than 0.061 higher than T5-XXL on negative log perplexity; by comparison, another 250k steps of T5-XXL improve it by only 0.052.
**But the large models also expose problems:**

list: **Switch-XXL is occasionally unstable**: the earlier tricks work for Base, Large, and C but not enough for it, so it was not trained for the full 1M steps.

**Upstream good doesn't mean downstream good**: The 1.6-trillion-parameter Switch-C scores only 87.7 on SQuAD, below the smaller Switch-XXL (89.6). On SuperGLUE, Switch-XXL, pretrained on about 503B tokens (about half of T5-XXL), scores 87.5, below T5-XXL's 89.3; but on knowledge tasks like closed-book QA, it exceeds previous best results. The paper's conclusion is that Switch's upstream gains transfer more readily to knowledge tasks, and less fully to reasoning tasks.

callout.title: More parameters, smarter model
callout.text: This paper is itself a counterexample. Switch-C has about 4x the parameters of Switch-XXL, but Switch-XXL applies far more compute per token and does better on downstream tasks like SQuAD. The paper's explanation: there is a "not yet understood" relationship among fine-tuning quality, per-token compute, and total parameter count. Roughly, more parameters is like "remembering more"; more compute is like "thinking harder"; the two are not interchangeable.

list: **One sentence gets the order backwards**: Section 3.1 says the 64-expert model "reaches at step 450k the level T5-Base reached at step 60k." Given the 7.5x speedup, it should be the reverse: Switch reaches at step 60k the level T5-Base reached at step 450k.
**"About 10x" is really about 7x**: Sections 5.6 and 8 both say Switch-XXL uses about 10x the per-token compute of Switch-C. According to Table 9, 6.3T / 890B is about 7x.

**"100x the parameters" is really about 17x**: Table 6's caption says a sparse model with "100x more parameters" can be distilled into a small model, but the table's teacher Switch-Base has 3.8B parameters and the student 223M, about 17x. The body's "about one-twentieth of the parameters" is closer.
**Attention head count doesn't match**: Table 1 says Switch-Base+ increases attention heads "from 14 to 16", but Table 9 lists 12 heads for both T5-Base and Switch-Base.
**"Lower is better" is backwards**: Table 11 in the appendix says negative log perplexity is "lower is better", but everywhere else in the paper it is higher is better (closer to 0 is better).

**Is the perturbation additive or multiplicative?** The appendix says it applies a "multiplicative" perturbation to the input, but the appendix pseudocode adds a random number near 1 to the routing scores.

sections.h: Afterward: MoE became a mainstream choice for large models

list: **Top-1 vs. Top-2**: Switch proved routing to a single expert can work; later many open-source MoE models returned to choosing two or more experts per token, plus finer-grained experts. The right number depends on trade-offs among quality, communication, and hardware.
**Load balancing remains a core issue**: Switch's auxiliary loss (α · N · Σ f P) became common practice. The final close read in this route, DeepSeek-V3, will look at a different approach.
**Stability tricks were widely adopted**: practices like high precision in the router and smaller initialization later became common in large-model training.
**"Upstream good, downstream not necessarily good"**: this phenomenon reminds us that evaluating sparse models by pretraining perplexity alone is not enough.

blocks.p: This route next changes direction, from "adding parameters" back to the Transformer's own parts: next up is **rotary position embedding (RoPE)**, which nearly all open-source large models use today to tell the model where each token sits.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: When each token is sent to only one expert, why can the router still be trained?
options: Because the expert's output is multiplied by the routing probability p_{i}(x), so gradients can flow back to the router through that multiplication
Because the router is fixed and doesn't need training
quiz.why: Earlier researchers thought at least two experts had to be compared for routing to be learned. The paper argues that once the output is multiplied by the gate probability, the router has a gradient, so k = 1 can learn.

quiz.q: What is the cost of setting the capacity factor too high?
options: More empty slots, wasting memory and compute, and increasing communication
quiz.why: A larger capacity factor drops fewer tokens, but each expert must allocate slots for its capacity; unused slots are waste. The paper finds Switch performs best at small capacity factors of 1.0 to 1.25.

quiz.q: Switch-C has 1.6 trillion parameters. Why does it underperform the 395-billion-parameter Switch-XXL on SQuAD?
options: Switch-XXL uses far more compute per token; the paper argues there is a not-yet-understood relationship among fine-tuning quality, compute, and parameter count, and more parameters cannot fully substitute for more compute
quiz.why: Section 8 of the paper is devoted to this "anomaly." It shows the advantages of sparse models are clearer on knowledge tasks, while reasoning tasks may still need more compute.

blocks.p: After this close read, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: How does a Switch layer differ from an original MoE layer? What are the benefits of k = 1?
What are expert capacity and the capacity factor? What happens to dropped tokens?
How is Switch's load-balancing loss computed? How does it encourage balance?
What problem does each of selective precision, smaller initialization, and expert dropout solve?
Compared with T5-Base and T5-Large, where does Switch gain its speed?
How much quality can distillation retain?
Why do we say "upstream good, downstream not necessarily good"?

main.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity (arXiv:2101.03961, v3)

sources.note: This close read is based on v3 of the arXiv paper (the content of the JMLR 2022 published version), first posted in January 2021. Tables marked "Illustrative" use our own numbers computed from the paper's equations. The "about 7x" and "about 17x" figures are our calculations from the paper's tables. Later open-source MoE practices come from public material and are not in the paper.
